source.name: Madam C. J. Walker
body: In the early 1900s, women across the country began opening their doors to saleswomen trained in the "Walker System" of hair care. These agents, nearly all Black women, sold products and taught techniques door to door. For many, it was the first chance to earn a good living outside of domestic or farm work. The woman behind the system was Madam C. J. Walker.

She was born Sarah Breedlove on December 23, 1867, in Delta, Louisiana. Her parents had been enslaved on a Madison Parish plantation, and she was the first member of her family born into freedom. Orphaned before age seven, she married young, was widowed, and moved to St. Louis, where she worked as a laundress and cook.

Like many women of the time, she suffered from scalp problems and hair loss. In 1904 she began using and selling the hair products of businesswoman Annie Turnbo Malone, then developed her own. In 1905 she moved to Denver, married Charles Joseph Walker, took the name Madam C. J. Walker, and launched her own business.

Her business grew quickly. She trained agents and taught her methods. In 1910 she moved her operations to Indianapolis and built a factory for her Walker Manufacturing Company. She organized her agents and encouraged them to be active in their communities. In August 1917 she held her agents' first national convention, at Union Baptist Church in Philadelphia, with more than 200 women attending; delegates telegrammed President Wilson to protest the East St. Louis riots.

Walker became one of the wealthiest Black women of her time, with a fortune that topped $1 million, and she may have been the first American woman to become a millionaire through her own work. She gave to the NAACP, the YWCA, schools, and orphanages, paid tuition for Black students at Tuskegee Institute, and supported the anti-lynching movement. She died in 1919 at her estate, Villa Lewaro, in Irvington, New York.

source.name: George C. Marshall
source.field: Military leadership, diplomacy and international affairs
body: On June 5, 1947, U.S. Secretary of State George C. Marshall spoke to the graduating class at Harvard University. Europe was still in ruins two years after World War II. In his speech Marshall proposed that the United States help rebuild it. That idea became the Marshall Plan.

Marshall was born in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, in 1880. He graduated from the Virginia Military Institute in 1901 and was commissioned a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army. President Franklin D. Roosevelt chose him as Army Chief of Staff, and he led the Army through World War II, reaching five-star rank in 1944.

After the war, he led a mediation mission to China in late 1945. President Truman then made him Secretary of State; he took office on January 21, 1947. Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act in March 1948 to fund the Marshall Plan, and aid eventually rose to more than $12 billion for rebuilding Western Europe.
The plan rested on an argument of its time: that U.S. security depended on the economic recovery and stability of its allies, not only on military strength.

Marshall left the State Department on January 20, 1949. He then served as president of the American Red Cross and, from 1950 to 1951, as Secretary of Defense. In 1953 he received the Nobel Peace Prize. He died on October 16, 1959, at Walter Reed General Hospital in Washington, D.C.

source.name: Maysoon Zayid
body: In January 2014 TED posted a talk with a title that gets a laugh on its own: "I got 99 problems ... palsy is just one." The speaker was Maysoon Zayid, a Palestinian American comedian from New Jersey who has cerebral palsy.

Zayid studied theater at Arizona State University. Early in her acting career she found she would get more work by doing stand-up, and TED quotes her telling the BBC that "a fluffy ethnic disabled chick was never going to get a job unless she did stand-up." In 2003 she and comedian Dean Obeidallah co-founded the New York Arab-American Comedy Festival.

She appeared in You Don't Mess with the Zohan and has a recurring role as the lawyer Zahra Amir on General Hospital, after two years early in her career on As the World Turns. Her first graphic novel, Shiny Misfits, published by Scholastic in 2024, centers on a disabled elementary school student.

By TED's account, she spends several months a year in the Palestinian territories running art workshops for disabled and orphaned children in refugee camps. New Jersey Monthly reported in 2020 that she lives in Cliffside Park.

source.name: Lana Barkawi
body: Each year in the Twin Cities, the lights go down in a theater and an audience settles in to watch films from across the Arab world and its diaspora. Before the first film starts, Lana Barkawi steps up to open the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival.

As of October 2026, Barkawi is the executive and artistic director of Mizna, the St. Paul arts organization profiled on this page. She publishes its journal, Mizna: SWANA Literature and Art, and produces the festival. SWANA stands for Southwest Asia and North Africa. Mizna's staff page notes that she holds a doctorate in biochemistry and links that training to her collaborative, discovery-based way of working. She has also served on grant panels for funders including the Knight Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts.

In 2019 Mizna marked 20 years of publishing, and public radio covered the anniversary. "I say every year when I open the film festival, it feels like our work is more important now than ever," Barkawi said. In April 2023 Mizna named Ellina Kevorkian deputy director to work alongside her, a hire tied to growth supported by a multi-year McKnight Foundation award.

source.name: Michael Aung-Thwin
body: In 2018 the National University of Singapore named a University of Hawaiʻi professor to its George E. Bogaars endowed professorship for 2018–2019, to teach Myanmar's history and give a public lecture. Michael Aung-Thwin had spent decades in American universities teaching the deep past of the country where he was born.

He was born in Yangon (Rangoon), Burma, in 1946. He went to high school at Kodaikanal International School in South India, then came to the United States for college. He earned a B.A. at Doane College in Nebraska, an M.A. at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and a Ph.D. at the University of Michigan.

His teaching took him to Elmira College, Kyoto University, Northern Illinois University and the National University of Singapore. He settled at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where he worked in the Center for Southeast Asian Studies and became Emeritus Professor of Asian History.

His books include Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma (1985), The Mists of Ramanna (2005), A History of Myanmar Since Ancient Times (2013) and Myanmar in the Fifteenth Century (2017). He died after a long illness on 14 August 2021 at his home in Hawaiʻi. His son, Maitrii Aung-Thwin, is also a historian of Southeast Asia. His family asked for donations in his memory to the Burma Studies Foundation.

source.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Colombian here covers people from the Andes, the Caribbean coast and the Pacific, Afro-Colombian and Indigenous people, and people who differ by generation, faith, education and immigration history. It also covers adoptees from Colombia raised in Minnesota, who may have little or no connection to what is below. We found no study of Colombian Minnesotans or Colombian Americans and disability, and none of Colombian adoptees in Minnesota. What follows comes from studies in Colombia and from one U.S. study of Latino parents in general, and each says which it is.
questions: How do you understand what is going on for you or your child? What words do you use for it at home?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or an assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who helps with care, and who would you like to be part of decisions?
Is your faith or church community a support for you? Would you like them involved?
What are your child's strengths, and what do you hope for their future?
Which language do you prefer for meetings and written materials: Spanish, English or both? If you sign, which sign language do you use?
If you were adopted from Colombia or grew up away from relatives there, what, if anything, would you like us to know about that?
Is there anything you want to know about who sees your information before we go further?
If you would like to tell me, did something in your life, such as an accident, an illness or a conflict, lead to this?

context.heading: What studies from Colombia have asked
body: A 2009 Colombian review (Castellanos Soriano and López) searched eight databases for articles from 1997 to early 2007 and selected 31 studies and literature reviews on disability and culture, not all from Colombia. It called the research "incipient," meaning just beginning. About 55 percent of the studies looked at how culture shapes the experience of families and caregivers. It says nothing about any one family.

A 2022 focus-group study with parents of autistic children in Colombia (Hughes, Magaña and colleagues) found four themes: how the diagnosis affected the family, systemic and societal barriers, the strengths parents saw in their child, and their hopes for the child's future. The abstract does not state how many parents took part. The authors recommended culturally responsive parent education.

Hughes, Magaña, Gonzales, Núñez and Moreno-Angarita, Journal of Special Needs Education 25(1), 2022

context.heading: A U.S. study of Latino parents, not Colombians
body: In a study presented in 2015, 34 Latino parents of autistic children aged 2 to 22 (59 percent Mexican, 15 percent Puerto Rican, 24 percent other) were interviewed at home and asked whether a child's condition is a message from God. Most described their child as a positive sign, such as a blessing, part of God's plan, or a test. Five saw the child as a punishment. Others pointed to nature, and some said the wider culture sees punishment but that they rejected that view. About half the families attended religious services at least a few times a year. It is a small sample and a conference abstract, and no Colombian result can be drawn from it. Ask, and do not assume either a faith or a medical explanation.

context.heading: Conflict, stigma and the gap between law and experience
body: A 2025 preprint from Colombia, not yet peer-reviewed (González Ballesteros and colleagues), looked back over qualitative research on psychosocial disability. It reported a consistent gap between legal protections and lived experience, especially for Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities affected by violence, and said that people with disabilities had limited part in processes such as peacebuilding. It describes Colombia, not people who have since moved. Some people who came from Colombia lived through conflict or displacement and others did not, so it is for the person to tell you, if they wish.

context.heading: Language and sign language
body: Rights documents in Spanish use "persona con discapacidad" (person with a disability), as Human Rights Watch does. Mariana Lozano describes herself as a woman with an intellectual disability. Ask each person which words they use.

Colombia's national institute for Deaf people, INSOR, works in Colombian Sign Language (Lengua de Señas Colombiana), recognized in Colombian law since 1996, and keeps a national registry of its interpreters. It is a different language from ASL, so ask rather than assume. Use trained interpreters, not children or relatives, and do not assume that someone from Colombia reads or speaks Spanish. An adoptee raised in Minnesota may speak only English.

context.heading: Fear of systems, and what we could not find
body: We found no study of Colombian families in the U.S. on fear of public systems. Immigration status may matter to any family, and it may not. Say only what your agency's current written policy supports about who sees a person's information, and do not make promises beyond it.

We also found no Colombian research on traditional healing and disability services, and no source on who in a Colombian family makes care decisions. Ask each family. Minnesota has no Colombian disability organization that we could find, and we could not find a Colombian American disability advocate with a public record. MPR News reports that Colombia Live's dancers include adoptees, and that families call it a second family, which is the closest thing to a Minnesota connection in this material.

source.name: Diane Guerrero
body: Diane Guerrero was 14 when she came home from school in Boston to find her parents gone. Immigration authorities had detained them in spring 2001, and they were deported to Colombia. She was a U.S. citizen, born in New Jersey on July 21, 1986. Publishers Weekly's review of her memoir says she was left "with no government oversight whatsoever." Friends and family took her in and helped her enroll at the Boston Arts Academy.

Kirkus Reviews reports that her parents entered in 1991 on a 90-day visitor visa and stayed past its end. Publishers Weekly adds that they tried to gain legal status and were defrauded by a con artist. In the memoir she describes the depression that followed, and the help she found when she confided in a therapist.

She became known for her roles on Orange Is the New Black and Jane the Virgin. In November 2014 she told her family's story in a Los Angeles Times op-ed. In 2016 she published In the Country We Love: My Family Divided, written with Michelle Burford, which won a 2017 Alex Award from the American Library Association. Publishers Weekly notes her work as a White House Ambassador for Citizenship and Naturalization, and Kirkus her volunteering for the Immigrant Legal Resource Center.

source.name: Juan C. Zapata
body: In 2002, voters in a Miami-Dade County district sent Juan Carlos Zapata to Tallahassee. His legislative profile lists him as the first Colombian American elected to the Florida Legislature.

That profile says he was born in Medellín, Colombia, on December 9, 1966, and moved to Florida in 1977. Miami Today, in a 2013 profile, says he was born in Peru to Colombian parents. Both agree on his family's Colombian roots and on 1977. He earned an associate degree at Miami-Dade Community College and a bachelor's degree from Florida International University in 1994. Before running for state office he chaired the West Kendall Community Council and served on Miami-Dade County's Equal Opportunity Board and Planning Advisory Board.

A Republican, he represented House District 119 from 2002 until term limits ended his service in 2010. He chaired the Miami-Dade Legislative Delegation and the Board of Hispanic Caucus Chairs. Nationally, he chaired the NALEO Educational Fund, the nonprofit arm of the National Association of Latino Elected and Appointed Officials, and a National Conference of State Legislatures committee. He then won a seat on the Miami-Dade County Commission, District 11, in 2012, and was still in that seat in May 2016. He no longer holds the seat; as of October 2026 the county lists Roberto J. Gonzalez as the District 11 commissioner.

source.name: Laura Redden Searing
body: During the Civil War, the St. Louis Republican sent a young Deaf woman to Washington, D.C., to report on politics and the military. Laura Redden interviewed President Abraham Lincoln, who also bought her books. Her readers knew her as "Howard Glyndon," a male pen name. By the National Deaf Life Museum's account she chose it because a man's name drew more attention, though her own name appeared beside it.

Laura Catherine Redden was born on February 9, 1839, in Somerset County, Maryland, by the State Historical Society of Missouri's account, which notes that some sources give 1840. Her family moved to St. Louis when she was a child, and spinal meningitis left her Deaf at about 11. She enrolled at the Missouri school for the deaf in Fulton in 1855. In 1858 she became editor of the St. Louis Presbyterian and began publishing in the Missouri Republican.

In 1862 she published Notable Men, biographies of members of Congress. Her 1864 collection Idylls of Battle and Poems of the Rebellion brought national attention. From 1865 to 1868 she studied languages in Europe and wrote for the New York Times and other papers. Back in New York she wrote for the Evening Mail and for magazines such as Harper's. From 1870 she studied speech and lipreading, including a year under Alexander Graham Bell, and in her articles urged that deaf schools teach speech along with sign language.

In 1872 she signed a petition supporting women's voting rights, and in 1875 she published a suffrage column in the Evening Mail. She married Edward Whelan Searing in 1876, had a daughter in 1880, moved to Santa Cruz, California, in 1886, and divorced in 1889. She died in 1923.

source.name: Maaza Mengiste
body: On September 15, 2020, the Booker Prize, one of the most prestigious awards for fiction in English, announced its six-novel shortlist. One was The Shadow King, by the Ethiopian-born American writer Maaza Mengiste. Its subject was Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, told through the women who fought it.

Mengiste was born in Addis Ababa and lived in Nigeria and Kenya before settling in the United States. She earned a B.A. at the University of Michigan in 1993 and an M.F.A. in creative writing at New York University in 2007, and has held a Fulbright scholarship and fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts and Creative Capital.

Her first novel, Beneath the Lion's Gaze (2010), is set in Addis Ababa during the revolution and the political violence that followed. The Shadow King (2019) reaches further back: a woman helps disguise a peasant as the emperor and becomes his guard, inspiring other women to take up arms. She also edited the anthology Addis Ababa Noir (2020).

Italy occupied Ethiopia from 1936 to 1941. Mengiste's books bring that history to a wide English-speaking audience while centering women left out of official accounts. She is a professor of English at Wesleyan University, after earlier posts at Princeton University and Queens College, and in 2026 she was named a MacArthur Fellow.

source.name: Barbara Mikulski
body: In 1969, highway planners wanted to run an East-West Expressway through the old Polish and working-class neighborhoods of East Baltimore. A young social worker named Barbara Mikulski helped found a group of residents to stop it. That neighborhood fight started her political career.

Mikulski grew up in Highlandtown, East Baltimore. Her immigrant grandmother opened a bakery, and her parents ran a neighborhood grocery store. She earned a master's degree in social work from the University of Maryland in 1965, and her first job was with Catholic Charities, working with children in foster care and group homes.

She won a seat on the Baltimore City Council in 1971. She served in the U.S. House from 1977 to 1987 and in the Senate from 1987 to 2017. She was the first Democratic woman elected to the Senate without first being appointed or succeeding her husband. In March 2012 she became the longest-serving woman in the history of Congress, and later that year she became the first woman to chair the Senate Appropriations Committee. President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015. In September 2026 current and former lawmakers gathered on Capitol Hill to mark her 90th birthday.

source.name: Norman Borlaug
body: In July 1944 a young plant scientist trained at the University of Minnesota flew to Mexico City to lead a wheat research program. Norman Borlaug became the scientist most associated with the "Green Revolution."

Borlaug was born on March 25, 1914, in Saude, Iowa, a Norwegian American farming community, to parents descended from Norwegian immigrants. In 1933, at age 19, he arrived at the University of Minnesota. Over the next nine years he earned a bachelor's degree in forestry and a master's and a doctorate in plant pathology, studying under Professor Elvin C. Stakman.

In Mexico, Borlaug and his colleagues bred wheat varieties that resisted disease and gave higher yields. In 1965 he helped send semi-dwarf wheat seed to Pakistan and India, at a time when both countries feared famine. By the Academy of Achievement's account, Pakistan became self-sufficient in wheat by 1968, and India in all cereal crops by 1974.

In 1970 Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize for his contributions to the world food supply. In 1986 he created the World Food Prize. Congress voted him its Gold Medal in 2006, and President George W. Bush presented it in the Capitol Rotunda on July 17, 2007. He died in Dallas, Texas, on September 12, 2009, at age 95.

source.name: Kay Ulanday Barrett
body: Kay Ulanday Barrett is a poet, performer and essayist. The Foundation for Contemporary Arts describes them as navigating life in the U.S. as a disabled, Filipinx-American, transgender queer person. They were born in Mackinaw City, Michigan, earned a B.A. in Gender and Women's Studies at DePaul University, and live in Rahway, New Jersey.

Their first poetry collection, When the Chant Comes, came out from Topside Press in 2016. Their second, More Than Organs (Sibling Rivalry Press, 2020), was a 2021 American Library Association Stonewall Honor Book and a 2021 Lambda Literary Award finalist. They won the 2022 Cy Twombly Award for Poetry, and in July 2024 the Ford and Mellon foundations named them a Disability Futures Fellow. Barrett uses the identity-first word disabled, and their writing and teaching center disability justice.

source.name: Rubio Rubín
body: In 2021, playing for Real Salt Lake, Rubio Rubín threw himself backward and struck a bicycle kick into the net against the San Jose Earthquakes. Major League Soccer later named it its 2021 Goal of the Year.

Rubín was born in March 1996 in Beaverton, Oregon, to a Guatemalan mother and a Mexican father. In 2012 he was named U.S. Soccer's Youth Player of the Year. From 2011 to 2015 he played 51 games for U.S. under-17, under-20 and under-23 teams and scored 20 goals. On November 14, 2014, at 18, he made his debut for the U.S. senior national team against Colombia. He went on to play seven senior games for the United States, all exhibition matches.
He played for FC Utrecht in the Netherlands (2014–2017), for clubs in Denmark and Norway, and for Tijuana and Dorados in Mexico. He joined Real Salt Lake for the 2021 season.

In 2022 FIFA approved his one-time request to switch his national team from the United States to Guatemala, his mother's birth country. Real Salt Lake quoted him saying that he wanted "to pursue my dream of playing in the World Cup." He played for the Charleston Battery in 2025, and on December 30, 2025, El Paso Locomotive FC of the USL Championship announced it had signed him.

source.name: Kalpana Chawla
body: In November 1997, the Space Shuttle Columbia lifted off on mission STS-87. One of its mission specialists, the prime operator of the shuttle's robotic arm, was Kalpana Chawla. With that flight she became the first woman born in India to travel to space.

Chawla was born in Karnal, India. She earned an engineering degree at Punjab Engineering College in 1982 and moved to the United States for graduate school. She earned two master's degrees at the University of Texas at Arlington (1984 and 1986) and a doctorate at the University of Colorado Boulder in 1988. After that she did research on airflow around aircraft for NASA projects and worked in private industry in California. She became a U.S. citizen in 1990.

NASA turned down her first astronaut application. She was accepted on her second try and began training in March 1995. On the 1997 mission she deployed the Spartan satellite. It malfunctioned, and crewmates had to recapture it on a spacewalk.

In January 2003 she launched again on Columbia, mission STS-107, a research flight on which she served as flight engineer and ran experiments on how flames behave. On February 1, 2003, the shuttle broke apart over Texas as it came back through the atmosphere, and all seven astronauts died. Investigators traced the disaster to foam that broke off and damaged the wing during launch.

source.name: Mitsuye Endo
body: On July 12, 1942, a lawyer in San Francisco filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court on behalf of a 22-year-old Japanese American woman held behind barbed wire. Her case would reach the U.S. Supreme Court.

Endo was born May 10, 1920, in Sacramento, California, the second of four children of Japanese immigrant parents. She took a clerical job with the California Department of Employment. After Pearl Harbor, the State Personnel Board moved to dismiss Japanese American state workers, and by spring 1942 she had lost her job. She was one of 63 fired employees who challenged their dismissals with the help of the Japanese American Citizens League and attorney James C. Purcell.

She was held at the Sacramento Assembly Center, then at Tule Lake in California, and later at Topaz in Utah. When the government offered her an early release, she turned it down so the case could go forward. On December 18, 1944, the Supreme Court ruled in Ex parte Endo, in an opinion by Justice William O. Douglas with no dissents, that the War Relocation Authority had no authority to hold citizens it conceded were loyal. Just before the decision, which had been leaked to government officials, the Army opened the West Coast again to Japanese Americans it deemed loyal.

Endo left Topaz in May 1945 and moved to Chicago, where she worked as a secretary for the Mayor's Committee on Race Relations. About two years later she married Kenneth Tsutsumi, and they raised three children. By Densho's account she rarely spoke about the case. She died in Chicago on April 14, 2006. She was inducted into the California Hall of Fame in 2024, and on January 2, 2025, she was posthumously awarded the Presidential Citizens Medal.

source.name: Eh Tah Khu
body: In 2011, a year after arriving in Minnesota, Eh Tah Khu took a job as a youth development coordinator at the Karen Organization of Minnesota, as it was starting its first youth program. Five years later he was its co-executive director.

Khu was born in Burma and moved to Thailand as a refugee because of political conflict. He earned a four-year degree from Kawthoolei Karen Baptist Bible School and College, then spent two years teaching and helping manage schools under the Burmese Migrant Workers Education Committee. He came to Minnesota in 2010 with his wife and son, and in his first months he got help from Marner Saw, who is also on this page.

He became Youth and Social Services program manager in 2013, became a U.S. citizen in 2015, and was named co-executive director in February 2016. In 2023 Twin Cities Business described him as one of the first nonprofit executives of Karen descent in the country. It reported that KOM grew from 18 to 35 employees under him and that he led its team serving newly arrived Afghan and Ukrainian refugees.

When Ler Htoo was promoted to sergeant in 2024, Khu told MPR News, "With law enforcement action taken against minority ethnic groups [in Myanmar], there's a lot of mistrust." He said that knowing community members who work in law enforcement helps build trust. That is one person's account, from his own work.

In June 2025, KOM announced that he would step down as co-executive director as he neared 15 years there, to pursue new opportunities, and that he would stay through December 31, 2025. In November 2025 its board named Alice Buckner executive director, and as of October 2026 KOM's staff page does not list him. His term on the board of the Council on Asian Pacific Minnesotans runs from June 2025 to January 2028. The council's page, as saved in May 2026, still used his old KOM title.

source.name: Mũkoma wa Ngũgĩ
body: In 2009 a short story called "How Kamau Wa Mwangi Escaped into Exile" was shortlisted for the Caine Prize for African Writing. Its author, Mũkoma wa Ngũgĩ, was building a career as a novelist, poet and scholar in the United States.

He was born in 1971 in Evanston, Illinois, and raised in Kenya. He came back to the U.S. for his education: a BA at Albright College, an MA in creative writing at Boston University, and a PhD in English at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. As of October 2026 Cornell University's Department of Literatures in English lists him as a professor.

His novels include Nairobi Heat, Black Star Nairobi, Mrs. Shaw and Unbury Our Dead With Song. He has also published poetry and the study The Rise of the African Novel: Politics of Language, Identity, and Ownership (2018). In 2013 New African named him one of the 100 most influential Africans. He co-founded the Mabati-Cornell Kiswahili Prize for African Literature, which rewards writing in an African language. He is a son of the writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, also on this page.

source.name: Chloe Kim
body: In February 2018, a 17-year-old from Southern California won Olympic gold in snowboard halfpipe in Pyeongchang, South Korea, her parents' home country. Chloe Kim became the youngest woman to win an Olympic snowboarding gold.

Kim was born in 2000 in Long Beach, California, and her hometown is Torrance. Her parents, Jong Jin and Boran Kim, moved to the United States from South Korea. Her father took her snowboarding at age four, bought her a secondhand board and drove her to Mammoth Mountain on weekends.

She won her first X Games gold in superpipe in 2015, at age 14, the youngest winner in the event's history at that time, and went on to tie Shaun White for the most halfpipe wins in X Games history, with eight. In 2019 she announced a break from competition to attend Princeton University, then returned to the sport. At the 2022 Beijing Olympics she won halfpipe gold again, the first woman to win back-to-back Olympic halfpipe titles.

At the 2026 Milano Cortina Games, Kim competed with an injured shoulder after a crash in Switzerland about a month earlier. She led after her first run but fell on her last two. Gaon Choi of South Korea, a 17-year-old she had mentored, won gold, and Kim took silver.

source.name: Wat Lao Buddhavas
body: In 1983, soon after the first Lao refugees arrived in Des Moines, the community bought a piece of land. The temple building was completed in 1997 and the rest of the grounds in 1999. Drake University's Comparison Project calls it the first Lao Buddhist temple in the city. Its two pages on the Des Moines temples spell the name Wat Lao Buddhavas and Wat Lao Buddhavath, and one explains that Wat Lao simply means Lao temple.

Drake describes a central temple with an altar, a residence for the monks, and two guest houses for visitors. Sunday services include chanting in Pali and a dharma talk in Lao, followed by a potluck. A Tak Bat, an offering of food to monks, is held about once a month, and an Ancestor's Day honors those who have died. Drake's guidance for visitors is to dress modestly, remove shoes, and not stretch your legs toward the altar or the monks.
By 2009 a second Lao temple in Des Moines, Wat Phothisomphan, had been established as a meditation monastery.

source.name: Saymoukda Duangphouxay Vongsay
body: Zombies, cannibals and spirits are not what most audiences expect from a play rooted in refugee history. That is the point. In Kung Fu Zombies Vs Cannibals and Kung Fu Zombies Vs Shaman Warrior, Saymoukda Duangphouxay Vongsay told stories of war and displacement through action and humor, making Twin Cities stages places where Lao stories could be thrilling as well as serious.

Vongsay was born in a refugee camp in Nong Khai, Thailand, just across the Mekong River from Laos. Her family resettled in Minnesota in the mid-1980s, and she is based in Saint Paul. She earned a BA in English from the University of Minnesota, Morris, in 2005 and a Master of Liberal Studies from the University of Minnesota in 2017.

Her writing moves across forms. Her book When Everything Was Everything reflects on childhood in a refugee family, and she has been developing a musical, In the Camps: A Refugee Musical. In 2020 she and Theater Mu, the Twin Cities' Asian American theater company, received an Andrew W. Mellon Foundation grant through the National Playwright Residency Program, making her a full-time playwright in residence at Mu for three years. She was named a 2022 Bush Fellow.

source.name: Bill Richardson
body: In 1995 a U.S. congressman sat down face to face with Saddam Hussein and won the release of two American aerospace workers held in Iraq. It was one of many such missions for Bill Richardson, who became one of the best-known American negotiators for people held abroad.

He was born on November 15, 1947, in Pasadena, California, to a Mexican mother and an American bank executive father, and grew up in Mexico City before being sent at 13 to school in Massachusetts. He earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts University in 1970 and a master's from its Fletcher School in 1971.

He represented New Mexico in the U.S. House from 1983 to 1997. President Clinton named him U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations (1997–1998) and then Secretary of Energy (1998–2001). He was governor of New Mexico from 2003 to 2011 and ran for the 2008 Democratic presidential nomination. Through the Richardson Center he kept negotiating for detained Americans, and in 2021 he secured the release of journalist Danny Fenster from prison in Myanmar. He died in his sleep on September 1, 2023, at his home in Chatham, Massachusetts.

source.name: Conrado "Conrad" Vega
body: When the Minnesota Senate convened in January 1977, one of its new members was a social studies teacher from Lakeville High School. Conrad Vega, a DFLer from Dakota County, is recorded by the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library as the first known Hispanic person to serve in the Minnesota Legislature.
Vega was born on June 22, 1938, in South St. Paul, and was of Mexican ancestry. South St. Paul's stockyards and meatpacking plants long drew working families to the city.

Voters elected him to the Senate in 1976. He served from 1977 to 1986, representing District 52 and then, after redistricting, District 39. He also served on the South St. Paul Economic Development Authority. He died on December 26, 2010, at age 72.

source.name: Huda Zoghbi
body: In 1999 a team in Huda Zoghbi's laboratory in Houston identified mutations in a gene called MECP2 as the cause of Rett syndrome, a severe neurological disorder that mostly affects girls. The finding made a simple genetic test for the condition possible.

Zoghbi was born Huda El-Hibri on June 20, 1954, in Beirut, Lebanon, and grew up there. She entered the American University of Beirut in 1973 and began medical school two years later. When the Lebanese Civil War made study in Beirut impossible, her parents sent her and her brother to stay with a sister in Austin, Texas, expecting them to return the next summer. The war went on. She finished medical school at Meharry Medical College in Nashville, a historically Black medical school, earning her M.D. in 1979.

In 1983 she joined Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital for a child neurology residency. As a clinician she saw children with Rett syndrome and turned to research. In 1993, working with Harry Orr of the University of Minnesota Medical School, she helped identify ATAXIN1, the gene behind spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), an inherited movement disorder. Her later work showed that the amount of MECP2 protein matters: too little causes Rett syndrome and too much causes a different disorder.

She became founding director of the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator. Her honors include the Shaw Prize (2016), the Canada Gairdner International Award (2017) and the 2022 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience, which she shared with Orr, Jean-Louis Mandel and Christopher Walsh. Lebanon awarded her its National Order of the Cedar in 2018.

1979: M.D., Meharry Medical College, after the civil war interrupted her studies in Beirut.

source.name: Héctor P. García
source.field: Medicine, civil rights and veterans' rights
body: In 1949, a funeral director in Texas would not let the family of Private Felix Longoria, a Mexican American soldier killed in World War II, hold services in the funeral home's chapel. A Corpus Christi doctor named Héctor P. García made the case public. Senator Lyndon B. Johnson helped arrange for Longoria to be buried at Arlington National Cemetery, and the case drew national attention to the discrimination Mexican American veterans faced.

García was born January 17, 1914, in Llera, Tamaulipas, Mexico, and moved with his family to Texas in 1918. He graduated as his high school's valedictorian and finished at the University of Texas in 1936. At UT's medical school in Galveston, a quota system left him the only Latino in his class. In 1942 he volunteered for the U.S. Army. He served in Europe and North Africa and received the Bronze Star.

After settling in Corpus Christi, García saw Mexican American veterans being denied the benefits they had earned. In 1948 he founded the American G.I. Forum to fight for them. The group also took on school segregation, the Texas poll tax and discrimination on Texas juries. He organized "Viva Kennedy" clubs in 1960. As an alternate U.S. delegate to the United Nations, on October 26, 1967, he addressed the General Assembly in Spanish, which a 2010 resolution of Congress describes as the first speech there by an American in a language other than English. On March 26, 1984, President Ronald Reagan presented him with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and that resolution calls him the first Mexican American to receive it. He died in Corpus Christi on July 26, 1996.

source.name: Eugenie Anderson
body: On October 12, 1949, President Harry Truman announced that he would send a farm wife from Red Wing, Minnesota, to Copenhagen as U.S. ambassador to Denmark. Eugenie Anderson became the first woman in American history to hold the rank of ambassador.

She was born Helen Eugenie Moore in Adair, Iowa. She met John Pierce Anderson at Carleton College, married him in 1930, and settled on his family's farm, Tower View, in Red Wing. A 1937 trip to Germany, then under Nazi rule, turned her toward the study of international relations.

Minnesota's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party was born from a 1944 merger. Anderson helped organize it with Hubert Humphrey and helped push Communist factions out of the new party in 1946–1947. By 1948 she was Minnesota's Democratic national committeewoman.

In Denmark she served from 1949 to 1953, and in 1951 she signed a U.S.–Danish treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation, the first woman to sign such a pact. Back home she chaired the Minnesota Commission for Fair Employment Practices from 1955 to 1960. President Kennedy sent her to Bulgaria in 1962, where she served until December 1964. She later represented the United States on the United Nations Trusteeship Council. She died in Red Wing on March 31, 1997.

source.name: Maria Sanford
body: In 1909, at age 72, Maria Sanford stood before graduates of the University of Minnesota to give the commencement address. MNopedia calls her the first woman to do so at a major university. For nearly thirty years she had taught rhetoric and oratory on the Minneapolis campus, and many had come to call her "the best-loved woman in Minnesota."

Sanford was born in Saybrook, Connecticut. At fifteen she asked her parents to let her use her dowry money to attend New Britain Normal School, a teacher-training school. She graduated with honors in 1855 and spent twelve years teaching in Connecticut. In 1867 she moved to Pennsylvania, where she narrowly lost a race for county superintendent of schools at a time when women could not vote.

In 1869 Swarthmore College hired her to teach history, which made her one of the first women professors in the nation, and in 1870 she became a full professor. In 1880 William Watts Folwell, president of the young University of Minnesota, recruited her. She lectured widely across the state, work that grew more important after a bad investment in the 1880s left her $30,000 in debt. She paid her way by speaking.

The University named its first women's dormitory, Sanford Hall, for her in 1910. In 1920 she was chosen to speak at the state's celebration of the Nineteenth Amendment. She died that April in Washington, D.C., during a speaking tour. In 1958 Minnesota placed her statue in the U.S. Capitol's Statuary Hall.

source.name: Ngozi Ezike
body: In the spring of 2020, as COVID-19 spread, Illinois residents tuned in to daily news conferences from Gov. J.B. Pritzker's administration. Standing with him was Dr. Ngozi Ezike, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, who gave her updates in English and then in Spanish.

Ezike was born in Los Angeles, the daughter of Nigerian immigrants. Her father hoped his firstborn would become a physician. She speaks Igbo and is fluent in Spanish and French, and also speaks Swahili. She graduated with honors from Harvard, earned her medical degree at the University of California, San Diego, and completed a residency at Rush Medical Center in Chicago. She is board-certified in internal medicine and pediatrics.

For more than 15 years she worked in Cook County's public health system, including inpatient care at Stroger Hospital, medical director of the Austin Health Center on Chicago's West Side, and medical director of the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center, where she helped write its health policies. In 2019 she became the first Black woman to lead the 143-year-old state health department, serving until March 2022.

On June 13, 2022, she became president and CEO of Sinai Chicago, which CBS Chicago calls the city's largest private safety-net hospital system. Austin Weekly News described her in that role in May 2024.

source.name: Julia Ioffe
body: In 1990 a seven-year-old girl and her family left Moscow, a month before she was to finish first grade, and came to the United States. Two decades later, Julia Ioffe was back in Moscow as a correspondent, explaining Russia to American readers.

Ioffe grew up in Columbia, Maryland, attended Beth Tfiloh Dahan Community School in Baltimore and graduated from Princeton in 2005 with a history major and a certificate in Russian studies. With a Fulbright scholarship she returned to Moscow in 2009 and spent three years reporting for The New Yorker and Foreign Policy. Her 2011 profile of Alexei and Yulia Navalny was recognized by the Livingston Awards for journalists under 35.

Her work has appeared in The New Republic, Politico, The Atlantic, The New York Times Magazine and The Washington Post, among others. In 2021 she became a founding partner of the media company Puck, where as of October 2026 she is Washington correspondent. In 2025 she published Motherland: A Feminist History of Modern Russia, from Revolution to Autocracy, which traces Russian history through women's lives, including those of her own family. It was a National Book Award finalist and won a National Jewish Book Award.

source.name: Claudia Castro Luna
body: In 2015 Seattle named Claudia Castro Luna its first Civic Poet, a post she held for about two years. She was then appointed Washington State Poet Laureate, serving from 2018 to 2021. In 2019 the Academy of American Poets named her one of its Poet Laureate Fellows.
Castro Luna was born in El Salvador. She earned a BA in anthropology from UC Irvine, an MA in urban planning from UCLA, and an MFA in poetry from Mills College.

Her books include the chapbook This City (Floating Bridge Press, 2016), Killing Marías (Two Sylvias Press, 2017), One River, A Thousand Voices (Chin Music Press, 2020), and Cipota Under the Moon (Tia Chucha Press, 2022). By its publisher's account, Killing Marías addresses each poem to a woman named María who was killed in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. Her memoir, The Flowers Along the Way, is announced as coming from Curbstone Press.
As of October 2026 she teaches at Seattle University's Matteo Ricci Institute and is on the Humanities Washington Speakers Bureau for 2025 to 2027.

body: On the night Barack Obama accepted the Democratic presidential nomination in 2008, Michelle Obama wore a dress by Thakoon Panichgul. The moment put a Thai-born designer raised in Nebraska in front of a national audience.

Panichgul was born in Thailand and moved with his family to Omaha, Nebraska, at age 11. Sources name different provinces as his birthplace. He earned an undergraduate business degree from Boston University, worked as a buyer for J. Crew, and then took an editorial position at Harper's Bazaar. From 2001 to 2003 he took tailoring classes at Parsons School of Design in New York before launching his own label, Thakoon, with a 14-piece ready-to-wear collection in September 2004, sold exclusively through Net-a-Porter. In 2006 he was one of three winners of the Vogue/CFDA Fashion Fund, and the CFDA nominated him for its Swarovski Award for Best Emerging Womenswear Designer. He has collaborated with Gap, Mango and Target, and he later designed a collection for the department-store chain Kohl's.

source.name: Vladimir Horowitz
body: In 1986, after 61 years away, Vladimir Horowitz sat down at a piano in Moscow. The recital was televised internationally. He had left in 1925 on a six-month visa to study in Germany and had never gone back.

Horowitz was born on October 1, 1903, in Kyiv, then part of the Russian Empire, the youngest of four children in a musical Jewish family. His mother, a pianist, was his first teacher. He entered the Kyiv Conservatory in 1912 and began giving concerts in 1920, partly to help support his family. Some older sources name Berdychiv as his birthplace, but his birth certificate names Kyiv.

He made his American debut at Carnegie Hall on January 12, 1928, and settled in the United States. He played at a 1943 war bond rally that raised more than $10 million. He withdrew from the stage several times, once for 12 years, and his return to Carnegie Hall on May 9, 1965, sold out in two hours.

President Reagan presented him with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on July 28, 1986. Deutsche Grammophon counts 24 Grammy Awards, and Musical World counts 25. He died in New York on November 5, 1989, four days after his last recording session.

source.name: Christine Ha
body: Christine Ha was born in Southern California in 1979 and spent most of her childhood in Houston. Her parents were Vietnamese refugees. In her third year of college, at about age 20, she began losing her sight. Doctors first thought it was multiple sclerosis. A few years later she was diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica, an autoimmune disease; Fox News reported the year as 2004. She is legally blind, and by her account in BrainHealth her limited vision has stayed about the same since 2007.

She kept cooking, in part to reconnect with her Vietnamese heritage. In 2012 she won season 3 of the U.S. television show MasterChef, as its first blind contestant, while finishing a graduate degree in creative writing. Her cookbook, Recipes from My Home Kitchen: Asian and American Comfort Food, came out in 2013. In 2014 she received the American Foundation for the Blind's Helen Keller Personal Achievement Award.

In July 2019 she opened The Blind Goat, a modern Vietnamese gastropub in Houston's Bravery Chef Hall, which was a James Beard semifinalist for Best New Restaurant in 2020. A second Houston restaurant, Xin Chào, followed.

source.name: Stephanie Murphy
body: When Stephanie Murphy was about six months old, her family fled Vietnam by boat. The boat ran out of fuel and drifted at sea until, as her family has described it, the U.S. Navy found them and helped bring them to a refugee camp in Malaysia. A Lutheran church later sponsored the family's resettlement in Virginia.

Murphy was born in Ho Chi Minh City on September 16, 1978. She grew up in Virginia, graduated from the College of William & Mary, and earned a master's degree in foreign service at Georgetown University. After the September 11 attacks she worked as a national security specialist at the U.S. Department of Defense, then later in business and as a university instructor in Florida.

In 2016 she defeated longtime Republican incumbent John Mica, in a central Florida district. She became the first Vietnamese American woman elected to Congress. As a Democrat she served three terms, from 2017 to 2023, and was known for her work on defense and on bipartisan, fiscally moderate coalitions.

c. 1979: Family escaped by boat; rescued and taken to a Malaysian refugee camp.
Worked as a national security specialist at the U.S. Department of Defense.
November 2016: Elected to Congress from Florida's 7th District, the first Vietnamese American woman in Congress.
2017–2023: Served three terms in the U.S. House.
source.connectToWork: Refugees often arrive with a sponsor who becomes the go-between. In your work, how do you make sure the person, not the helper, is the one you are hearing from and answering to?
